final_answer:
Short answer: neither office has an inherent advantage because of the district; what maximizes the Guidelines range is ONE comprehensive indictment that captures the fraud in both states, brought by whichever office (D.S.C. or S.D. Ga.) can properly lay venue for counts covering both states' claims. Two separate indictments would not add prison time under the Guidelines.

1. Guidelines mechanics. Section 1347 fraud is sentenced under USSG §2B1.1, which is driven by loss. Fraud counts are grouped under §3D1.2(d) and loss is aggregated across the group. Relevant conduct under §1B1.3(a)(2) reaches uncharged acts that are part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan, so a judge in either district can count the other state's false claims in the loss figure and offense level, whether or not charged there. Thus the guideline range is essentially the same whichever district sentences, if the other state's conduct is related conduct (and a proven pattern of false claims across practices likely is). Separate prosecutions do not stack: under §5G1.3 (b)/(c) the second court generally imposes a concurrent (or adjusted) sentence for conduct already counted as relevant conduct in the first, so splitting the case yields no extra time and may cause double-counting disputes and litigation risk (and the second sentencing court can adjust for time served). A single case also avoids the possibility that the second case is treated as grouped/concurrent anyway.

2. Circuit-law differences are largely neutralized. Historically the Fourth Circuit (D.S.C.) deferred to the §2B1.1 commentary's 'intended loss' (United States v. Boler, 4th Cir. 2024, applying Kisor), while the Eleventh Circuit (S.D. Ga.) in United States v. Dupree (en banc 2023) refused deference to commentary that expanded 'loss', limiting loss to actual loss, which favored defendants there. Effective Nov. 1, 2024, Amendment 827 moved the 'greater of actual or intended loss' definition into the guideline text, which removes the Dupree/Kisor problem for post-amendment sentencing (subject to ex post facto analysis if the Manual in effect at sentencing is harsher than at offense; the offense conduct date matters). Therefore, to the extent any circuit-based edge remains for pre-Nov. 2024 conduct, it favors D.S.C. (Fourth Circuit) as the more government-friendly forum on intended loss, and the Eleventh Circuit's Dupree is less favorable to the government. I could not independently verify Dupree's current treatment within the budget.

3. Venue constrains the choice. Each execution of the health care scheme is a separate offense (§1347), and venue (Const. art. III §2, amend. VI; Fed. R. Crim. P. 18) lies where the offense was committed; for continuing offenses 18 U.S.C. §3237(a) allows venue in any district where the offense was begun, continued, or completed. A single district can prosecute both states' conduct only if it has venue for each count (e.g., claims submitted to or paid by a payor located in, or processed through, that district, or a single scheme/conspiracy spanning it). If the Georgia claims have no nexus to South Carolina (and vice versa), each office can charge only its own state's claims, and Rule 20/21 transfer (with defendant consent) would be needed to consolidate. In that case the practical recommendation is: the office that has venue over the larger-loss/more-serious portion, or a payor nexus covering both, should indict, and the other conduct should be brought in as relevant conduct, because judge will use aggregate loss anyway.

4. Statutory maxima. §1347 carries 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death), so with multiple counts consecutive sentences are possible under §5G1.2(d) if the guideline range exceeds a single count's max; charging many counts in one indictment maximizes available stacking, which a split would not.

Bottom line: indict once, in the district with venue over both states' claims; if only one such district exists, that office should indict. If both have venue equally, D.S.C. (Fourth Circuit) is marginally preferable on intended-loss law for pre-Nov. 2024 conduct. I am hedging because the question lacks facts on where claims were submitted and the dates.

claims.text: A single sentencing court can count the other state's fraud as relevant conduct and aggregate loss, so splitting indictments does not increase the guideline range.
Venue limits a district's ability to charge the other state's claims; the best choice is the office with venue over both states' claims.
Boler (4th Cir.) versus Dupree (11th Cir.) intended-loss differences are largely mooted for post-Nov. 2024 sentencing by Amendment 827; D.S.C. is marginally favorable for earlier conduct.
